books.title: Talk Like TED
books.author: Carmine Gallo
books.dek: The 9 public-speaking secrets of the world's top minds. Your notes, chapter by chapter.

chapters.title: Unleash the Master Within
summary: Passion beats expertise. Viewers can tell if you care, and they're not stupid.
Your passion isn't skincare. It's helping young guys improve their lives while entertaining them.
Passion spreads: positive, charismatic people lift and persuade others. Hire for it.

sections.title: Be passionate
sections.md:
If you're not passionate about the thing you're speaking about, how is the audience going to care? It's not about being an expert as much as it is about being passionate about it, and **showing** that you're passionate. The viewers can tell. They're not stupid.

==It's not really about being passionate about the product.== It's not about being passionate about skincare, but about helping young people improve their lives while entertaining them.

sections.title: What makes your heart sing?
sections.md:
Ask yourself that question. It's a stronger version of "what are you passionate about?"

::: key
**What makes my heart sing?**
Helping people improve the way they feel about themselves, so they can be themselves, express themselves however they like, and live happy in their teens and twenties.
I'm also passionate about entertaining others with my content: them reacting to it and liking the way I've made it.
:::

If your motivation for making the video is making money through it, it'll be hard to connect with your audience.
==If your motivation is to share your passion and improve other people's lives, you will connect with them.==

sections.title: Passion spreads
sections.md:
- If you're charismatic, you influence others. If you're happy and charismatic, you make others happy too. So a charismatic person who's passionate about something makes others a bit more passionate too. (Studies show it.)
- Positive leaders are more likely to influence an audience than negative leaders, and more likely to persuade followers to do what they want: buy a product, subscribe, eat more grilled cheese.
- The behaviour of leaders changes the happiness and well-being of their followers by influencing their emotional lives.
- It's not that success leads to happiness. **Happiness creates success.**

sections.title: Invite passionate people into your life
sections.md:
> "When you are surrounded with people who share a collective passion around a common purpose, anything is possible."

Use passion as a hiring criterion when you hire people to work on the YouTube channel with you. It's probably the most important one.

> "If it's your passion, then inevitably you'll succeed."

ideas: Know in one sentence what you actually care about (what makes your heart sing), and let that be why you make each video.
Viewers can tell whether you care. Show your enthusiasm instead of claiming it.
Motivation matters: wanting to help people connects with them, wanting money from them doesn't.
Enthusiasm and positivity spread to viewers and teammates, so choose passionate people to work with.

chapters.title: Master the Art of Storytelling
summary: Stories hit emotion first, then logic. Logic alone can't persuade: you need ethos, logos and pathos.
On your channel, pathos is small moments every few seconds. It must be painful not to watch to the end.
Every story has a hero, a villain and townspeople. People want humans, vivid words and someone to root for.

sections.title: Ethos, logos, pathos
sections.md:
Telling a story before you try to make the audience agree with you works, because it hits emotionally first and then logically. "Tell stories to reach people's hearts and minds."

Storytelling is the ultimate tool of persuasion. Brands and people who tell stories (emotional, genuine stories) connect with their audiences in a far deeper, more meaningful way than their competitors.

Aristotle believed persuasive communication happens when three things are present:
- **Ethos:** credibility (achievements, title, experience)
- **Logos:** logic, evidence, data and statistics
- **Pathos:** appealing to emotions

[[fig:persuasion]]

To persuade means influencing someone to act by appealing to reason. But according to some of the most logical minds in the world, ==you simply cannot persuade through logic alone.== You need emotion.

sections.title: Small emotions, every few seconds
sections.md:
On your channel there's a lot of pathos, just not in the usual way. It isn't long emotional stories. It's **small moments every few seconds**:

[[fig:beats]]

- **Curiosity:** "There's one exception…"
- **Surprise:** "I expected this to work, but it didn't."
- **Humour**
- **Suspense:** "We'll come back to this."
- **Relief:** "The good news is…"

sections.title: Break the pattern, open a gap
sections.md:
Personal stories make the brains of the storyteller and the listener sync up: "brain-to-brain coupling". Personal stories with an **unexpected result** are the most compelling (an idea the book takes from Made to Stick).

The most basic way to get someone's attention is to **break a pattern**. Curiosity and mystery grab us. Curiosity happens when we feel a gap in our knowledge. Gaps cause pain: we want to know something but we don't, and to take the pain away we need to fill the gap.

::: key
**It must be painful not to watch the video through to the end.**
:::

When you have a dream in your heart, you know you're going to succeed. Every fail means you're one step closer to winning.

sections.title: People want people
sections.md:
Famous neuroscientists believe we're hardwired for empathy: it's the social glue that holds society together. In a video you create empathy by talking about yourself or about someone else.

> "The truthful, inside story of almost any man's life, if told modestly, is most entertaining. It is almost sure to be good speech material."

==Improving your appearance is not about becoming worthy. It's about removing the barriers that stop you from expressing yourself.==

People like seeing the person who makes the product. That's why KFC has a face, and why you like IcePro and Jawliner. Humans want to see stories of other humans. ==That's why AI-voice YouTube channels can't build a community.==

Every brand and every product has a story. Find it and tell it.

sections.title: What a story is
sections.md:
Jonah Sachs (*Winning the Story Wars*): stories are a kind of communication designed to persuade an audience of the storyteller's worldview. The storyteller puts characters, real or fictional, on a stage and shows what happens to them over time. Each character pursues a goal according to their values, faces difficulty along the way, and succeeds or fails according to the storyteller's view of how the world works.

Audiences today are bombarded with messages, so they're more resistant and sceptical than ever. But when a story inspires them, they spread it for you, and that creates a massive viral effect.

**A hero story** is about one person's success. Your audience wants someone or something to cheer for. They want to be inspired. Give them a hero: yourself, other people, or successful brands.

sections.title: Hero, villain, townspeople
sections.md:
::: blue
Every story has a hero and a villain.
- **The hero** is my product, brand or idea.
- **The villain** is a challenge (like ascending), or the dark side of the community I stand against, or the people who hate the whole idea.
- **The townspeople** are my audience. The hero saves them from the villain, and they live happily ever after.
:::

[[fig:story]]

Give the audience at least one character to root for.

sections.title: Persuade people to join you
sections.md:
To succeed, you have to persuade others to support your vision, dream or cause.

Example, looking for a YouTube team at BUas. Tell a story:

> "You go to university to become a great editor. You come here for 4 years, you pay the university every year, you pay for accommodation and live in this city, and in return you learn a lot about media, and editing is one part of it. But imagine you could work with a successful channel, taught by the editor exactly how to edit, nothing else. These videos get uploaded and you get feedback from real viewers, a lot of them. At some point you edit completely on your own and become a master. You get all of this for free, unlike university. And if you stick with it long enough, you can make a very good amount of money while being part of a cool YouTube team. I'm offering it because I think you're a very cool person and good at editing. Together we can become very successful on YouTube."

Compare that to: *"Hey bro, you know I have a YouTube channel. I really need an editor, but I'm not gonna pay you at all, if that's not a problem. Can you help?"*

sections.title: Vivid words, no clichés
sections.md:
Avoid overused buzzwords and clichés. People hear them all the time, so they've lost their meaning. They get ignored, they're meaningless, and they're boring.

When you describe things people can touch or smell, their sensory cortex activates and they subconsciously feel it. So use metaphors, analogies and vivid language, but no clichés: your audience tunes out phrases they've heard a million times.

**An experiment:** a guy bought cheap objects, wrote a story about each one, and sold them. He spent $127 and sold them for $3,240, because they had stories. Stories raised the value by about 25×.

::: check
It's a real project (Significant Objects). But it's about selling objects, so it doesn't mean a story-video gets 25× the views. "Stories add a lot of value" is the honest version.
:::

ideas: Hit emotion first and logic second: stories persuade, facts alone don't. You need credibility, evidence and emotion together.
On your channel, emotion means a small beat every few seconds (curiosity, surprise, humour, suspense, relief), not one long sad story.
Open a curiosity gap and make it hard to stop watching before it closes.
Give every story a hero, a villain and someone to root for. Personal stories with an unexpected result work best.
Use concrete, vivid words and skip clichés.
When you recruit people, tell the story of what they gain, not "can you help me for free".

chapters.title: Have a Conversation
summary: Practise until delivering the script feels like an exciting conversation with a close friend.
If your voice, gestures and body don't match your words, people stop trusting the message.
Gestures free and natural, an eager style, real feedback, and no fidgeting.

sections.title: The rule: talk like a friend
sections.md:
::: blue
**Practise relentlessly and internalise your content, so you can deliver it as comfortably as having a conversation with a close friend.**
Your note: "Read this again." If you practise the content until you can tell it comfortably, isn't this one of the most important things for your scripts? Yes.
:::

**Why it works:** true persuasion happens after you've built an emotional rapport with your listeners and gained their trust. If your voice, gestures and body language don't match your words, your listeners will distrust your message.

The problem with most technical or scientific presentations is that the presenter fails to make the content visual, interesting and entertaining.

sections.title: Your voice
sections.md:
Get the speed, volume, pauses, emphasis and pitch right for each part of the script. How should you say this next sentence? Is it important? Are you going to let it breathe?

One TED speaker with great pacing (not the fastest, but the best speed for each moment) said he isn't reading to you, he's having a conversation with you. He imagines talking to a friend over dinner in a restaurant.

==In my first video I wasn't speaking in a conversation tone.== That's not how a conversation sounds. It should sound like a conversation, but an **exciting** one: my voice needs to be a lot higher and stronger for the viewer to hear it as normal. Other than that, make it a conversation.

sections.title: Believe what you say
sections.md:
If you don't believe in what you're saying, your body or voice will show it. There's no way to hide it unless you're a trained FBI agent. So believe in your message: don't spread lies, be a firm believer in what you're saying, and show it.

The way you dress, carry yourself and talk is how the audience decides whether to believe you and care. The book says criminals who've shot police officers chose officers who weren't dressed sharp: slouching, bad posture, unconfident. But audiences spot fake confidence too: they've been trained by thousands of videos.

::: check
The police example comes from an FBI interview study with a small number of offenders. Treat it as a story, not proof.
:::

sections.title: Real feedback
sections.md:
Ask many different types of people for real feedback on your video:
1. What did you like most?
2. What did you like least?
3. What did you remember?

The book's three Ps: **Passion, Practice, Presence.**

sections.title: Gestures and body language
sections.md:
Complex thinkers use complex gestures. When somebody is passionate about a topic, he gestures with his hands even if he tries not to.

Pay attention to what your body is saying. Walk, talk and look like a leader people want to follow, in real life too, not just in videos. Learning to command presence (people listen to you, believe you and care about what you say) is charisma and leadership practice. It helps the channel, and it matters when you get people to work with you.

Direct tips from the book:
1. **Use gestures.** Let your hands be free.
2. **Use them sparingly.** Gestures should be natural. Don't think about which to use; your story will guide them.
3. **Use them at key moments.** Save your most expensive gestures for the key moments.
4. **Keep them above the waist.** You want people looking at your eyes, hands and upper body.

Also: stand straight, make eye contact, and wear colours that pop from the background.

sections.title: Eager vs reserved
sections.md:
If you want to make your request or offer more attractive, an **eager** nonverbal style works better.

[[fig:eager]]

- **Eager:** very animated, broad open movements, hands projected outward, leaning forward.
- **Reserved:** leaning back, slower and smaller movements, slower speech.

When you're trying to make a point, cut every mannerism that serves no purpose: playing with a pen, tapping your fingers, spinning around. But move a bit. Don't stay completely still.

sections.title: Before you film
sections.md:
The way you pose changes how you see yourself. Before a speech, if you're alone for 2 minutes, stretch your arms out confidently and take up space: the "power pose".

::: check
The book says it raises testosterone and lowers cortisol. That part failed to replicate (Ranehill 2015). Feeling a bit more confident is the honest claim, so don't put the hormones on camera.
:::

To get your energy up before a speech, jump around, open your body up, and move.

**A staging idea:** one TED speaker with an injury put five chairs next to each other on stage. Each chair was one part of her story: chair 1 the accident, chair 2 the ten days in hospital, and so on. A visual that improves the storytelling.

ideas: Rehearse until you can say the script like an exciting conversation with a friend, with more energy than normal talking.
Voice, face and body must match your words, or viewers stop trusting you. Believe what you say.
Gestures: free, natural, above the waist, saved for key moments. Cut fidgeting that does nothing.
An eager style (animated, open, leaning in) persuades better than a reserved one.
Ask test viewers three questions: what did you like most, least, and what do you remember?
Warm up before filming by moving and taking up space.

chapters.title: Teach Me Something New
summary: The brain is wired for novelty: new information, a new package, or a new way to solve an old problem.
Surprise them (the blue/red pattern interrupt) and teach something they can use in daily life.
Know the one big thing, in one sentence that fits in a title. Big picture before details.

sections.title: Why novelty works
sections.md:
Recognising novelty is a hard-wired survival tool all humans share. Our brains look for something brilliant and new, something that stands out, something that looks delicious.

**Teach me something new.** Reveal information that's completely new to your audience, package it differently, or offer a fresh way to solve an old problem.

**Why it works:** the brain loves novelty. An unfamiliar, unusual or unexpected element intrigues the audience, jolts them out of their assumptions, and quickly gives them a new way of looking at the world.

sections.title: Your pattern interrupt
sections.md:
Something I thought of, and it's true:

::: key
Talk about (imaginary) blue and red as if blue is the good one, or let the audience assume blue is healthier. Then ask "so which one should you get?" and answer **"red, because…"**.
The moment you say red, they're shocked. Their mind was careless: they weren't listening deeply because they thought they knew what you'd say. The surprise makes them listen harder, remember the moment and get curious.
:::

sections.title: Teach what they can use
sections.md: The audience wants to learn new things, ideally things they can use in daily life. When I watch Rorz, I want to see something new I should do. That's the only reason I watch: the hope of learning something I can do. ==Teach your audience something they can do that improves their day-to-day life.==

sections.title: The brain's save button
sections.md:
Dopamine gets triggered artificially by gambling and drugs, but a healthy way to get it is learning new information. When something new is rewarding, we tend to remember it, because the brain marks it as important.

How do you use that? Make the information new and exciting. The best teachers keep finding new ways to deliver the same information. Novelty creates enthusiasm in both the teacher and the audience. Get them addicted to learning.

YouTube shows this perfectly: a new type of thumbnail gets you excited and shows information in a new way. When everybody copies it, it stops working, because you've seen it. Then a new type appears and works again.

::: check
Novelty does help memory. "Learning is the best way to get dopamine" is the book's framing, not an established fact.
:::

sections.title: Package it differently
sections.md:
Package your ideas well, especially scientific ones. How can you show it in an interesting visual way? Hans Rosling's moving country bubbles turned boring statistics into a famous talk.

Study successful strategies outside your field: other niches, and other things entirely. If someone speaks persuasively, you can learn from him whether or not he has a YouTube channel.

Old communist buildings repainted in bright colours: same buildings, same people inside, but one looks depressing and the other looks modern and safe. ==Repackage the idea, not just the title and thumbnail.==

Every audience wants a new way to solve its problems. We're wired to look for them.

sections.title: Be a purple cow
sections.md:
We're bombarded with information, and even good stuff gets skipped if it's basic: we've heard it before. Packaged differently, we listen. Have a remarkable style, like Aprilynne Alter: so simple, yet so remarkable.

[[fig:cow]]

If you see a cow on the road you don't care. A purple cow, you're amazed. Only purple cows, you don't care again. **Be remarkable.**

Put your own spin on things. Don't just copy formats. The brain needs something it has never processed to break out of predictable perceptions.

sections.title: Beginner's mind: one big thing
sections.md:
::: key
Can you describe your idea in one sentence? If someone asks a viewer "what was this guy talking about?", he should have one clear answer. One big thing.
Ask: **"What is the one thing I want my audience to know?"** Make sure it fits in a YouTube title.
:::

The audience needs the big picture, then the details. A caveman who meets a tiger doesn't ask how many teeth it has. He asks if it's going to eat him. People need to know **why** before **how**: why we debloat before increasing daily potassium.

ideas: Teach something new, or package something old in a new way. Novelty is what the brain remembers.
Use a pattern interrupt: let them assume the obvious answer, then say the opposite and why.
Teach something they can use in daily life.
Repackage the whole idea, not only the title and thumbnail. Borrow formats from other niches and stay different when everyone copies.
Know the one big thing as a single sentence that fits in a title. Give the why before the how.

chapters.title: Deliver Jaw-Dropping Moments
summary: One shocking, unexpected moment can define a whole talk (Gates' mosquitoes, under 5% of the time).
Emotionally charged events and things that feel important get remembered.
Five ways to create one; end on a showstopper.

sections.title: Bill Gates' mosquitoes
sections.md:
Bill Gates gave a TED talk about malaria. He opened a jar of mosquitoes and said poor people shouldn't be the only ones to experience this. (He later said they weren't infected.) It probably scared some of the crowd, making them feel a little of what people in Africa feel. People reposted it with headlines like "Bill Gates releases swarm of mosquitoes on TED audience".

==It took less than 5% of his talking time, and it's remembered years later.==

Identify the most important points you want to make in the video. Then find a novel, memorable way to deliver them. Sometimes you need to surprise your audience to make them care.

sections.title: Plan the moment first
sections.md:
Before scripting, know what the story is: what makes it interesting, what the format is, and how it's packaged.

Use several senses while planning: seeing, touching, feeling. Stand at a whiteboard, pick up a pen, draw on the laptop, think while walking. Anything that engages more areas of your brain.

Every memorable story, film or presentation has one scene that everyone remembers because it's so impactful.

sections.title: Why it works: emotional events
sections.md:
Psychologists call it an **emotionally charged event**. Gates hooked his audience because it was shocking, unexpected and different, and our brains are wired to remember that kind of moment.

People remember exactly what they were doing when 9/11 happened, who they were with and where, 25 years later. But they don't remember where they left their wallet this morning. One was emotionally charged; the other wasn't.

Emotionally charged = shock, surprise, fear, sadness, joy, wonder.

::: check
The book puts the amygdala in the prefrontal cortex and says it releases dopamine. It's actually in the temporal lobe, and it strengthens memories with stress hormones like noradrenaline. Also, 9/11 memories feel vivid but aren't perfectly accurate. The main point is right: emotional moments get remembered.
:::

sections.title: Importance makes memory
sections.md:
Higher perceived importance gets remembered more. So if someone talks to the YouTuber personally in the Discord, he's far more likely to remember his videos 5 years from now.

I still watch Maurits's videos because I texted with him for one minute, four years ago.

sections.title: 5 ways to create a wow moment
sections.md:
[[fig:wow]]

1. **Props and demos**
2. **Unexpected, shocking statistics**
3. **Pictures, images and videos**
4. **Memorable headlines:** a repeatable line you say. Craft and deliver quotes people repeat.
5. **Personal stories**

sections.title: End on a high note
sections.md:
A showstopper: a mind-blowing moment that seals the deal and brands the message into people's minds. One singer ended her concert by zip-lining across the whole stadium.

So: deliver jaw-dropping moments. It can be a short story, a video, an image, a statistic, something emotional.

ideas: Plan one jaw-dropping moment for each video before you write the script. It can take only a few seconds.
Emotionally charged moments (shock, surprise, wonder) and things that feel important get remembered.
Five ways to make one: a prop or demo, a shocking statistic, a picture or clip, a repeatable line, a personal story.
End on a high note.

chapters.title: Lighten Up
summary: Humour plus novelty is gold. Don't take yourself or your topic too seriously.
Humour lowers defences and makes you likable; funny people get seen as smarter and more stable.
Humorous observations, mostly about yourself, not jokes. Five types. Balance humour, stats and shock.

sections.title: Why humour works
sections.md:
The most popular TED talk ever ("Do schools kill creativity?") has one novel thing about it: humour. We love humour. We love novelty. Combine the two and you've got presentation gold.

**Don't take yourself (or your topic) too seriously.** The brain loves humour. Give your audience something to smile about.

**Why it works:** humour lowers defences. It makes you more likable, and people watch and buy from people they like.

Facts and content on their own are unemotional. You need to package them emotionally, with humour and surprise. Humour is one of the keys to making a message novel.

sections.title: How to use it
sections.md:
Humour is powerful, but you have to use it creatively and naturally. Repeating stupid jokes has the opposite effect. Use it when it actually fits. It's a skill.

::: key
**Make humorous observations instead of telling jokes**: something small, related to what you're talking about.
The humour must not distract from the video. It should **amplify** your words by making people more awake and energised, and so more focused on what you're saying.
:::

==One of the best ways: make the humour about you.== You did something stupid, not your competitor.

sections.title: Humour as a social skill
sections.md:
A good sense of humour is a social skill we admire. Understanding your topic is one thing; having a good sense of humour is another. Combining the two is stronger than relying on one.

- Studies show we attribute other good traits to people with a good sense of humour: friendly, considerate, pleasant, interesting, intelligent, emotionally stable.
- Laughter doesn't just carry information. It spreads positive emotions to others, which makes them more favourable toward the person laughing.
- Humour reduces hostility, deflects criticism, relieves tension, improves morale, and helps communicate difficult messages.

In dating, the book says humour ranks as the most important thing in almost every survey, above career success, education and even physical attraction. That's why you see female superstars dating average funny guys.

::: check
Humour ranks very high in what people *say* they want. But what people say and who they actually choose often differ (speed-dating studies), so don't claim on camera that it beats looks.
:::

sections.title: 5 ways to use humour
sections.md:
1. **Anecdotes and observations:** short stories or examples meant to put a smile on people's faces, not to get a huge laugh.
2. **Analogies and metaphors:** a comparison that shows how two different things are alike. Excellent for explaining complex topics.
3. **Quotes:** funny ones, or ones you comment on in a funny way. Don't grab random famous quotes; do your homework. They can come from anyone, including people you know.
4. **Videos**
5. **Photos**

sections.title: Balance and be yourself
sections.md:
Balance humour, statistics and shock.

Don't take your topic too seriously, and especially don't take yourself seriously. Be authentic and don't try to be something you're not.

==If something made you laugh, there's a big chance it'll make others laugh too.==

ideas: Make humorous observations, mostly about yourself, instead of telling jokes.
Humour should amplify the message, not distract from it.
Five tools: anecdotes, analogies, quotes, clips, photos.
Balance humour, statistics and shock, and stay yourself.

chapters.title: Stick to the 18-Minute Rule
summary: About 18 minutes is a good rough length. Heavy thinking tires people, so cut what doesn't need to be there.
Explain it simply. Making things complex is easy; simple takes genius and courage.
Use the rule of 3, and build a message map: one headline, 3 messages, support for each.

sections.title: About 18 minutes
sections.md:
> "You have to be really courageous about your instincts and your ideas. Otherwise you'll just knuckle under, and things that might have been memorable will be lost."

The 18-minute rule is just a good rough timing.

The book says thinking uses glucose, so a lot of thinking makes you physically tired, and that resisting food, watching a presentation and solving a maths puzzle all draw on the same source of energy.

::: check
That "same energy source" idea (ego depletion) failed a big 23-lab replication. The useful part stays true: heavy, dense content tires viewers, so keep it lean.
:::

sections.title: Simple takes courage
sections.md:
> "If you can't explain it simply, you don't understand it well enough." (usually credited to Einstein)

::: key
Explaining a complex topic simply is something to strive for every time. People who don't are scared they won't show every little thing they know. When I make a video, the idea isn't to show my audience "look, I know all these complicated things". **It's to inform them in an easy and meaningful way.**
:::

> "Any intelligent fool can make things bigger and more complex. It takes a touch of genius, and a lot of courage, to move in the opposite direction."

That one is usually credited to E. F. Schumacher, though it often gets quoted as Einstein. Either way: courage.

sections.title: The rule of 3
sections.md:
::: key
**Splitting things into 3 always works.** If needed, split each of those 3 into 3 again. Do it as much as possible.
:::

[[fig:rule3]]

It's everywhere:
- My flag has 3 colours.
- You eat with a spoon, knife and fork.
- The US Declaration of Independence has 3 famous rights: life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.
- Obama's crowds shouted 3 words: "Yes we can."

It's much easier to take in an idea in 3s.

Another rule-of-3 trick: show 3 things where **the 3rd is the bad one**, or where only the 3rd is good. Don't show them all at once, but one at a time: 1, 2, 3 (surprise). Ryan Trahan does this.

sections.title: The message map
sections.md:
A message map is a very effective communication tool. Use it often. It makes sure your idea is organised.

**Step 1: the headline.** Ask "What is the single most important thing I want my viewer to know about my product, service, brand or idea?" The answer is your headline, e.g. "eat whole foods", "start doing cardio", or "read Atomic Habits and write notes in a notepad". It must be under 140 characters, and shorter is usually better.

**Step 2: support the headline with 3 key messages.** For "eat whole foods": (1) sodium consumption worldwide, (2) the problem with processed foods, (3) what to do instead.

**Step 3: reinforce each message with stories, statistics and examples.** For sodium worldwide: (a) WHO's recommendation vs the world average, (b) what it does to your body, (c) a personal example.

[[fig:message-map]]

The book's example is a message map of Steve Jobs's 2005 Stanford commencement speech, made by the Gallo Communication Group. The speech is built exactly like this: one headline and three stories.

[[fig:jobs-map]]

ideas: Dense content tires people. Cut anything that doesn't earn its place.
Explain things simply. Showing off what you know is easy, simple takes courage.
Split everything into threes. When you show three things, make the third the surprise.
Build a message map before scripting: one headline under 140 characters, three key messages, proof for each.

chapters.title: Paint a Mental Picture with Multisensory Experiences
summary: The brain ignores boring, single-sense content. Pair your words with visuals, especially for beginners.
Paying attention to two things at once is a myth: a simple visual he understands beats a cool edit he can't follow.
Pictures beat words for memory. Mix visual types, balance facts with feeling, and let key numbers stand alone.

sections.title: Touch more than one sense
sections.md:
Deliver presentations with parts that touch more than one sense: sight, sound, touch, taste and smell.

**Why it works:** the brain doesn't pay attention to boring things. Reading plain text, for example, is boring, and it touches only one sense. The brain craves multisensory experiences.

So my videos shouldn't be only verbal, but also visual (images, videos, animations), for a better learning experience.

==Visual + verbal matters most for people with no prior knowledge of the topic.== People who already know it can build the mental model themselves.

sections.title: Multitasking is a myth
sections.md:
::: purple
**When it comes to paying attention, multitasking is a myth.** The brain can't do it well.
So don't try to impress with cool animations. Use simple visual storytelling the viewer can always actually understand.
If you have 2 choices:
1. A really cool edit or visual, but it's a bit too fast and it's hard to focus on what you're saying.
2. Skip the cool edit, and the viewer understands what you're saying.
**Always choose the second.**
:::

[[fig:choice]]

This is biology: we can't pay attention to more than one thing at a time. So what do we do instead? Neuroscience gives us the next idea.

sections.title: Pictures beat words
sections.md:
**The Picture Superiority Effect (PSE):** pictures are superior to words. The book quotes John Medina: "Human PSE is truly Olympian."

[[fig:pse]]

The usual result: when it comes to remembering information later, pictures demolish text and speech. ==Use visuals to enhance your words.==

sections.title: Mix your visuals
sections.md:
::: blue
Charts are good, but chart after chart after chart gets boring. Break the video up with different types of visuals, while still sticking to one specific style. Keep the right balance of both.
:::

When you show statistics, at some point show an individual human with that problem. The viewer's brain gets a break from the charts, and it shows how important the point is. A statistic is data. A picture of the person in the statistic is not just data, it's emotion. You need a balance of facts and emotions.

sections.title: How do you want them to feel?
sections.md:
Don't think only about what you want people to know. **Think about how you want them to feel.**

Today I watched a guy who used to be really ugly and is now very attractive and a model. From what he said, I could tell he knows far more about attractiveness than I do. It gave me a feeling of hope: "yes, I can change, anybody can change how they look." One of the top comments was "anybody can become an 8".

That feeling of hope and security made me remember him better, because now I know I can get even better, and that I can help others improve dramatically, night and day. You get that feeling from seeing someone's before and after.

sections.title: Let one thing stand alone
sections.md:
If I want something highlighted in the viewer's brain, I can show it **on its own for 2 seconds**. If I say "200 people die every month from too much sodium", put a big "200" on screen on a plain background and stay silent for a second. It amplifies the effect, and the viewer actually gets to feel it.

[[fig:alone]]

==That's why intense, fast editing isn't always the answer.==

::: check
The 200 is an example number for the technique, not a real statistic. Use a real, sourced number when you do this in a video.
:::

ideas: Pair words with visuals, especially for viewers who are new to the topic.
Choose understandable over cool. Never edit so fast that viewers can't follow what you say.
Pictures are remembered better than words. Vary the visual types inside one style, and follow a statistic with a real person.
Decide how you want viewers to feel, not only what to know.
Let one key number sit alone on a plain screen for a second or two.

chapters.title: Stay in Your Lane
summary: Be authentic, open and transparent. Most people can spot a phony.
The goal of a video isn't "a video made". It's to move people, and they only move if they trust you're real.
Practise your content until it's automatic, so you can deliver it like yourself.

sections.title: People can spot a phony
sections.md:
**Be authentic, open and transparent.**

Why it works: most people can spot a phony. If you try to be something or someone you're not, you'll fail to gain the trust of your audience.

Successful people identify their life's core purpose and relentlessly follow it, to become the best version of themselves they can be.

sections.title: The goal of a video
sections.md:
When you're making a video, the goal is not for "a video to be made". ==The goal is to inspire your audience, to move them, and to encourage them to dream bigger.==

You cannot move people if they don't think you're real. You'll never convince your audience of anything if they don't trust, admire and genuinely like you.

sections.title: Practise until it's yours
sections.md:
Practise telling your content. With repetition it becomes more automatic, and you can focus on delivering it in a more interesting, authentic way.

::: key
Rehearsing doesn't make you sound scripted. Not rehearsing does, because your attention goes to remembering words instead of your face, voice and energy. Know it well enough that you can talk like you're explaining it to a friend (chapter 3).
:::

sections.title: End of the book
sections.md:
You don't need luck to be an inspiring speaker. You need **examples, techniques, passion and practice**.

You also need courage: the courage to follow your passion, say your ideas simply, and show what makes your heart sing.

[[fig:ted9]]

ideas: Be real. Viewers spot phonies, and they won't be moved by someone they don't trust.
The goal of a video is to move people and make them dream bigger, not to get a video made.
Rehearse until it's automatic, so your attention is free to be yourself on camera.

books.title: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
books.author: Stephen R. Covey
books.dek: Character first, technique second. Your notes so far: the Foreword and Inside-Out.

chapters.title: Foreword
summary: A great company (or channel) needs two things: preserve the core AND stimulate progress.
The core is a set of principles you never trade away. It sets the direction.
Progress is everything else: change and improvement.

sections.title: Preserve the core, stimulate progress
sections.md:
A great company needs two things:

==Preserve the core AND stimulate progress.==

- **The core:** a set of principles you keep no matter what. They give you guidelines for the direction you're moving in, as a company or as a channel.
- **Progress:** change and improvement in everything else.

[[fig:coreprogress]]

::: book
The foreword is by Jim Collins. "Preserve the core and stimulate progress" is the main idea of his own book, *Built to Last*: the companies that lasted kept their values fixed and changed everything else.
:::

::: key
For your channel: the core is evidence-based, safe, and honest about what doesn't work. Progress is formats, editing, packaging, thumbnails, your set. Experiment as much as you want on the outside. Never on the core.
:::

ideas: Keep a fixed core of principles you never trade away, and change everything else freely.
For your channel: the core is evidence-based, safe and honest. Formats, editing, packaging and set are what you experiment with.

chapters.title: Inside-Out
summary: The Character Ethic (who you are) is primary. The Personality Ethic (image, techniques) is secondary.
A paradigm is a map in your head. With the wrong map, trying harder or thinking positive won't get you there.
We see the world the way we've been conditioned to see it, so two people can look at the same thing and both be "right".

sections.title: Character Ethic vs Personality Ethic
sections.md:
Covey read through about 200 years of American "success" writing and noticed a shift.

- **The first ~150 years: the Character Ethic.** Success came from character: integrity, humility, courage, justice, patience, hard work, simplicity, modesty, the Golden Rule.
- **After World War I: the Personality Ethic.** Success came from personality: public image, attitudes, behaviours, skills and techniques. Smile more, think positive, use these influence tricks.

His point: ==the modern world is too focused on the Personality Ethic.== Techniques aren't useless, but they're secondary. Without character underneath, they come across as manipulation, and over time people see through them.

[[fig:iceberg]]

- **Character Ethic is primary.**
- **Personality Ethic is secondary.**

Character is who you really are.

> "What you are shouts so loudly in my ears I cannot hear what you say."

That line is usually credited to Ralph Waldo Emerson. ==What we ARE communicates far more than what we say or do.==

::: book
Covey's comparison: you can't cram on a farm. You can't forget to plant in spring, slack off all summer, then work hard in autumn and expect a harvest. Character works like a farm: it grows over time, and there's no shortcut.
:::

sections.title: Covey's son
sections.md:
Covey tells a story about one of his sons. The boy was struggling: behind at school, socially immature, small and clumsy at sports. Others laughed at him.

Covey and his wife tried the Personality Ethic. Positive mental attitude, cheering him on ("Come on, you can do it!"), telling off anyone who laughed at him. It didn't work. He kept failing and lost confidence.

Then they noticed what was underneath. ==The way they *saw* him was "inadequate, behind, needs fixing".== All the encouragement carried that hidden message, and he felt it.

So they changed how they saw him, not the technique. They stopped trying to fix him, worked on their own motives, and started enjoying and valuing him for who he was, letting him grow at his own pace.

Over time he blossomed: socially, at school and at sports, without being pushed.

==The change came from a new map of their son, not from a new technique.==

::: key
For your channel: viewers feel how you see them. If your picture of the viewer is "ugly guy I need to fix", it leaks into the script however nice the words are. Picture a guy who's already fine and can get better.
:::

sections.title: A paradigm is a map
sections.md:
Character Ethic and Personality Ethic are both **social paradigms**: ways a whole society sees success.

A paradigm is the way you see the world. Not in the sense of eyesight, but how you perceive, understand and interpret it. ==The simplest way to think of a paradigm is as a map.==

Imagine you're trying to get to a specific place in central Chicago. But the map you've been given is actually a map of Detroit. You have the wrong map.

- **You work on your behaviour.** Try harder, double the work, don't sleep. You only get lost faster.
- **You work on your attitude.** Stay positive. You're still not at your destination. You just don't care as much.

The problem might not be your behaviour or your attitude. **It's the map.**

[[fig:wrongmap]]

Once you have the right map of Chicago, your behaviour and attitude matter. But the map comes first.

We all have maps in our heads, of two kinds:
- **The way things are** (reality)
- **The way things should be** (values)

The way we think and act comes from these maps. We rarely question them. We just assume the way we see things is the way they are.

::: key
YouTube version: if your map says "views come from better editing", you can edit harder forever. Your Thumb Lab found hits and flops differ by concept and packaging, not pixels. Fix the map, then grind.
:::

sections.title: Young woman or old woman?
sections.md:
Look at the picture before you read on. What do you see?

[[fig:oldyoung]]

Covey describes a class at Harvard Business School. The instructor showed half the class a drawing of a young woman and the other half a drawing of an old woman, for about ten seconds. Then everyone saw this combined picture.

Almost everyone saw what their first picture had trained them to see. The arguments started. Each side was sure the other was blind, until someone traced the lines on the picture and it clicked: "Oh, now I see it!"

What Covey wants you to take from it:
- ==Your conditioning shapes what you see.== Ten seconds was enough. Years of family, school, friends and your feed do far more.
- Two people can look at the same thing, disagree, and **both be right** from their own map.
- Seeing the other side is a **paradigm shift**: suddenly you can't unsee it.

> "We see the world, not as it is, but as we are."

Covey adds: or as we are conditioned to see it.

ideas: Character comes first and technique second. Techniques without character read as manipulation, and people see through it.
There are no shortcuts for character. It grows over time, like a farm.
If results are bad, check your map (how you see the problem) before working harder on behaviour or attitude.
The way you see someone leaks into everything you say to them. See viewers as people who are fine and can get better.
Two people can look at the same thing and both be right from their own conditioning, so try to see the other side before you argue.

books.title: Made to Stick
books.author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
books.dek: Why some ideas survive and others die. Your notes so far: the Introduction and Simple.

chapters.title: Introduction: What Sticks?
summary: The movie-popcorn story: "37 g of saturated fat" became "worse than a whole day of junk food", and it changed an industry.
Ideas that stick share 6 principles: Simple, Unexpected, Concrete, Credible, Emotional, Stories.
The villain is the curse of knowledge: once you know something, you can't imagine not knowing it.

sections.title: The movie popcorn
sections.md:
Someone had to tell the world that movie-theatre popcorn is really bad for you. A medium bag had **37 g of saturated fat**. The US government recommended no more than **20 g a day**.

He could have made a chart showing it's almost double. Instead he said:

==A medium bag of movie popcorn has more artery-clogging fat than a bacon-and-eggs breakfast, a Big Mac and fries for lunch, and a steak dinner with all the trimmings, combined.==

He showed it visually too, side by side.

[[fig:popcorn]]

It ran on every TV news channel because the idea was packaged so well. People stopped buying popcorn at movies nationwide, and theatres stopped using coconut oil, so a healthier option appeared. His idea stuck.

::: book
The man was Art Silverman, at the Center for Science in the Public Interest, in 1992. The press conference showed the whole day of food spread on a table next to one bag of popcorn.
:::

sections.title: What makes people care
sections.md:
Emotion: fear, disgust, suspicion. These make the audience care.

==If it's something real from their daily lives that affects them, they care.== Nobody has feelings about "37 grams". Everyone has feelings about the popcorn in their hand.

sections.title: Spot ideas with natural potential
sections.md:
You need to learn to spot good ideas: ideas that naturally have high potential.

Think of basketball. There are short guys who are great at basketball, but if I had to pick random people for my team, I'd pick the 7-foot guy.

Still, a fast, athletic, trained 5'9" player will beat a clumsy 7-foot Discord mod. ==So spotting naturally good ideas matters, but then you have to learn how to turn them into great ones.==

sections.title: The 6 principles
sections.md:
*Made to Stick* found 6 principles behind ideas that stick.

[[fig:success]]

**1. Simple.** Create ideas that are simple but profound. Become a master of exclusion. If you watch a video with 10 ideas, even if they're all good, you won't remember one. Best case: one sentence so profound you could spend a lifetime learning to follow it.

**2. Unexpected.** Be counterintuitive. A bag of popcorn being worse than a whole day of junk food is counterintuitive. Surprise and emotion raise alertness and grab attention, but surprise is short-term. ==For an idea to last, you need interest and curiosity==, and you get them by systematically opening gaps in people's knowledge and then closing them.

**3. Concrete.** How do we make ideas clear? Explain them in terms of human actions and sensory information: things you can see, touch, taste.

**4. Credible.** How do we make people believe our ideas?

::: book
Not only with experts. The Heaths list other ways: vivid, specific details; statistics shown at human scale (like the popcorn); and "testable credentials", where the audience can check it themselves ("try this and see"). For you: show the before and after, show the study, let them test it on their own face.
:::

**5. Emotional.** How do we get people to care? We make them feel something. The movie popcorn makes them feel disgusted. The statistic "37 grams" doesn't.

**6. Stories.**

::: book
Stories get people to act. The Heaths say a story works like a flight simulator: hearing it is mental practice for the real situation. It also inspires. Three story plots that work again and again: the **challenge** plot (an underdog beats the odds), the **connection** plot (people bridge a gap), and the **creativity** plot (someone cracks an old problem in a new way).
:::

sections.title: Tappers and listeners
sections.md:
One person thinks of a song and taps its rhythm on a table. The listener has to guess the song.

Of 120 songs tapped, listeners guessed **3**. The tappers had predicted listeners would get **half**.

[[fig:tappers]]

Prediction: 1 in 2. Outcome: 1 in 40.

It's the same when scripting videos and presenting ideas. One of YouTube's rules again:

==Don't underestimate your viewer's intelligence, but don't overestimate their prior knowledge.== What sounds obvious to me might be completely new to a viewer.

This is the **curse of knowledge**: once we know something, we can't imagine what it's like not to know it. The tapper hears the song in his head. The listener hears knocking.

::: book
This was a 1990 Stanford study by Elizabeth Newton. The tappers aren't stupid; they just can't "un-hear" the tune. That's the whole problem with experts explaining things.
:::

ideas: Ideas that stick are simple, unexpected, concrete, credible, emotional and told as stories. Check every video against the six.
Make numbers human. "More fat than a whole day of junk food" beats "37 grams".
Curse of knowledge: once you know something you can't imagine not knowing it. Assume viewers know less than you think.
Don't underestimate viewers' intelligence, but don't overestimate what they already know.

chapters.title: Simple
summary: Find the core: the one thing that matters most. Highlight it and tell viewers it's the one.
Southwest's core: "we're THE cheap airline". Anyone in the company can make a decision with it.
Use simple language. Compact ideas (proverbs, "looksmaxxing") carry a lot in a few words.

sections.title: Highlight the most important thing
sections.md:
Highlight the most important thing, and **tell the viewers that it is**.

If there's one big thing to remember, the viewer is more likely to remember anything at all from the video.

In a video it's probably good to communicate the core message first.

sections.title: What is your core?
sections.md:
What is my core? In my situation, kind of my niche.

Southwest is an airline. Their core is "we are the cheap airline". From there, every decision comes from the same question: ==Does this help us be the cheapest airline? If not, we don't do it.==

The idea is simple not because it uses easy words, but because the commander's idea can be followed by the workers in unscripted situations. They just ask themselves: "Does this help us be the cheapest airline?"

Wizz Air employees would have to ask "Is this something Wizz Air would want?" How do you answer that? No idea.

::: book
The Heaths' example: someone in Southwest's marketing suggests adding a chicken Caesar salad on a popular route because passengers would like it. The answer: will the salad make us THE low-fare airline? If not, no salad. The army calls this **commander's intent**: one clear goal that still works when the plan falls apart.
:::

::: key
Write your channel's version as one question you can check every video against. Something like: "Does this help an average guy look better, with evidence, safely?" If a topic, sponsor or edit doesn't pass, cut it.
:::

sections.title: Simple beats specific
sections.md:
When we're deep into a topic, we want the more specific things, and we see the specific as more valuable (curse of knowledge). The audience wants a simple, easy explanation of their problem. They don't want to put a lot of effort in, unless they're deep into it too.

- Use simple language.
- Don't overcomplicate.

sections.title: Compact ideas
sections.md:
Compact ideas are good. Can you communicate an idea in very few words?

Proverbs do exactly that:
- "A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush."
- "С един куршум два заека" (one bullet, two rabbits).

Ideas that would take a long time to explain, made into a few words anyone gets.

Another example: ==**"looksmaxxing"**: one word for becoming more physically attractive as a guy, especially facially.==

ideas: Find the one thing that matters most, say it first, and tell viewers it's the one.
Write your channel's core as one question you can check every video against.
Choose simple over specific. Viewers want an easy explanation of their problem.
Compact ideas travel. A single word or proverb can carry a whole concept.

books.title: Feel-Good Productivity
books.author: Ali Abdaal
books.dek: Feeling good makes you productive, not the other way round. Your notes, sorted into the book's chapters.

chapters.title: Play
summary: When you don't want to do a task, ask: "What would this look like if it were fun?"
Do it for the process, not the end result. The result comes much later.
Rewards can kill the fun: people who just played kept going; the paid ones stopped.

sections.title: What would this look like if it were fun?
sections.md:
When I don't want to do a task, I ask myself: ==**"What would this look like if it were fun?"**==

Make the boring task fun:
- Add music
- Add humour
- Add a creative element
- Do it with friends
- Promise yourself a treat at the end

sections.title: Do it for the process
sections.md:
Do everything for **the process**, not the end result.

I love making YouTube videos. Ideating, packaging, scripting, filming, editing, analysing: that's what I love. Good connections and being able to afford cool stuff are a bonus I get later, not the reason I work today. ==If I think about the result, I won't enjoy the process==, because the result comes a lot later.

sections.title: See the task as a game
sections.md:
A study had two groups do the same puzzle. One group was told they'd get paid; the others were just asked to solve it. The second group did better: they saw it as a game and enjoyed the process instead of focusing on the end result.

==Seeing the "task" as a game helps a lot.==

::: check
The classic version is Edward Deci's 1971 study, with a block puzzle (a Soma cube) rather than a Rubik's cube. What changed wasn't who solved it. After the payments stopped, the paid group played with the puzzle far less in their free time than the unpaid group. The lesson is the same: pay for something fun and it starts to feel like work.
:::

ideas: When you don't want to do a task, ask "what would this look like if it were fun?" and add music, humour, a creative twist, company or a treat.
Do it for the process, not the result, because the result comes much later.
Be careful with rewards. Paying yourself for something you enjoy can turn it into work.

chapters.title: Power
summary: Believe you can do it: confidence that you'll manage makes you start.
Teaching others is one of the best ways to learn.
Own it. Not "I have to do this" but "I choose to do this".

sections.title: Believe you can
sections.md:
You have to believe in yourself and know that you can do the thing.

::: book
Ali calls this *self-efficacy*: your belief that you can pull something off. It grows from small wins, from seeing people like you do it, and from encouragement. Pick tasks you can win, then raise the bar.
:::

sections.title: Learn by teaching
sections.md:
A good way to learn is to teach others. ==Research shows teaching something helps you learn it better than studying it alone.==

That's partly why Rep Room has the "Teach the viewer" and "Teach your editor" drills.

sections.title: Own it: "I choose to"
sections.md:
Try to own the thing you're doing. If you don't own it, own *the way* you're doing it. Owning makes you want to work harder.

If you don't own the process at all, own your mood and the way you see it.

==Not "I have to do this". "I choose to do this."== Because everything I do, I choose:
- I want to do YouTube, so I choose to work on it.
- I want to make money, so I choose to go to work.
- I want to look good, so I choose to go to the gym.
- I want to be attractive, so I choose to take care of myself.
- I want to eat healthier, so I choose it.

ideas: Believe you can do it. Pick winnable tasks first, then raise the bar.
Teach what you're learning, because teaching beats studying alone.
Replace "I have to" with "I choose to", because everything you do is a choice.

chapters.title: People
summary: Work with people who give you energy. A team in sync pushes you forward; one slacker kills it.
Helping others and small acts of kindness make you feel good, and make you want to work harder.
Ask for small favours, face to face. React big to other people's good news.

sections.title: Work with others
sections.md:
Working with a group of people is proven to be a lot better. Do YouTube with others when you can.
- Make each other accountable.
- Work as a team, don't race each other. Set it up so that you working means all of you win, and them working means all of you win.

Some people drain your energy and some people give you energy. Find the ones who give it and ignore the ones who drain it. Make the others happy and yourself happy.

When you do a task alone it's easier to give up. A team pushes you forward: you're not alone, and you see the purpose.

sections.title: Be in sync
sections.md:
Be in sync with the others and you'll like each other and want to help each other. If you both work hard on the YouTube, that's sync. ==If one is working hard and one isn't doing anything, the sync dies, and now you're angrier than if you'd been alone.==

Even if you're not working on the same thing, working next to someone helps. Another YouTuber scripting his video next to me while I script mine would help me focus, even if he's doing maths homework. Now I'm supposed to be scripting, not doing random stuff.

sections.title: Helping makes you feel good
sections.md:
A way to feel good about your work is helping others. That's why volunteers like volunteering and why MrBeast likes helping people: it makes you happy and makes you want to work harder.

That's a reason I like my niche: ==it helps people.==

Small acts of kindness make you and others feel a lot better. Ali's example from when he was a doctor: on his way to get tea, he'd ask his colleagues if they wanted some.

sections.title: Ask for help
sections.md:
Asking others for a small favour often makes **them** feel better.

It works especially on "enemies". Ask someone you don't get along with for a favour. It's totally unexpected, and they might start liking you.

Benjamin Franklin had a rival in the legislature with opposite views. He asked to borrow a rare book from the man's library, then returned it with a warm thank-you note. The rival started treating him kindly, and they became friends for life. I know this from my own life too. It's a bit like "learn how to use enemies" from *The 48 Laws of Power*.

==Ask face to face. It's far more likely to get you the help you asked for than asking online== (probably because of the effort they see, and they can read your face).

If it's something they care about, say something like "I saw you're really good at… can you help me with this?"

::: check
The face-to-face study is real: Bohns and Roghanizad found requests made in person worked about **34 times** better than the same request by email.
:::

sections.title: When someone shares good news
sections.md:
When someone tells me positive news about themselves, ==react with energy and positivity==. I usually do the exact opposite, so this is important.

Swedish saying: "Shared joy is a double joy. Shared sorrow is half a sorrow."

::: book
Psychologist Shelly Gable calls the good reaction *active-constructive*: ask questions, get excited with them, let them relive it ("No way! How did it happen?"). A flat "nice" or changing the subject hurts the relationship more than you'd think.
:::

ideas: Work next to people who give you energy and cut back on people who drain it. Make working together a win for everyone.
Helping others and small kindnesses make you feel good and want to work.
Ask for small favours, in person. People like helping, even people you don't get along with.
React with energy when someone shares good news.

chapters.title: Seek Clarity
summary: Don't fight with motivation and discipline. Remove the block (the stone in your shoe).
Ask "why" 5 times to see if a task matters, then "how", with NICE goals.
If you don't know *when* you'll do it, you won't. Put it in the calendar.

sections.title: Unblocking, not motivation
sections.md:
Ali sees motivation and discipline as treating the symptoms, not the root problem. His method is **unblocking**, and he thinks it beats both.

His example: you have a little stone in your shoe and you have to get to dinner on time. Motivation and discipline is running there, arriving on time, and the ambulance comes because your foot is bleeding. ==Unblocking is taking the stone out of your shoe.== The goal gets easier.

sections.title: The 5 whys
sections.md:
When you want to do something, ask yourself why. What outcome do you want? To succeed you need clarity on what you're doing and why, otherwise you're just doing random stuff.

Before starting a new task or project, ask "why?" 5 times. The first answer is a short-term reason. ==By the fifth why, it should lead to something important to you long-term.==

[[fig:fivewhys]]

My example: I'll buy *Talk Like TED*.
1. Why? So I can read it and learn the info.
2. Why? So I can speak better.
3. Why? Because it'll improve how I speak to camera.
4. Why does that matter? I'll get more views and get better at YouTube.
5. Why does that matter? My goal in life is to become a great YouTuber.
6. Why? I love making videos, I'll have financial freedom, and I'll have fans I feel a personal connection with.

I even needed 6 whys.

If the whys don't lead anywhere, the task might be a waste of time:
- I want to watch a Minecraft video. Why? I like those videos. Why? It's a good game and the editing is cool. Why does that matter? It gives me dopamine. **Skip it.**

sections.title: Then ask how: NICE goals
sections.md:
Knowing why isn't enough. Then ask **how?** How can I reach this goal? ==Not knowing exactly what to do drains all your energy and wastes time.==

Goals are easier to reach when they're **NICE**:
- **N – Near-term:** goals you can work on soon.
- **I – Input-based:** measure the actions you take, not the results.
- **C – Controllable:** goals that depend on your own behaviour.
- **E – Energising:** goals that motivate and excite you.

Don't think too much about the long-term goal while you work, or you won't appreciate the short-term stuff. The 5 whys might say I'm making a video because I want 1 million subscribers by 2036. But during the task, think about the creating, not the subs. They aren't coming soon, so they won't give satisfaction. You love creating.

sections.title: When, exactly? Block time
sections.md:
==If you don't know *when* you're going to do the thing, you probably won't do it.==

**Time blocking:** put the work in your calendar. That time is now for that work, nothing else, so you'll do it.
- Start small: 1 hour a day for 1 thing. If it works, expand to more hours or the whole week.
- Dedicate time to working on YouTube, and to getting better in your niche.
- ==Don't block "YouTube time"==, because then you don't know WHAT to do. Block "scriptwriting the skincare video".

ideas: Remove the block instead of forcing it with motivation and discipline.
Ask "why" five times. If it never leads to something that matters to you, skip the task.
Then ask "how". Goals should be near-term, input-based, controllable and energising.
Decide when you'll do it. Block time for a specific task, not "YouTube time".

chapters.title: Find Courage
summary: Name the fear: "What am I feeling, and why am I scared?" Most fears run out of reasons.
Nobody's watching you as closely as you think (the spotlight effect).
An alter ego can do what you don't dare to. And ask 10/10/10: will it matter in 10 years?

sections.title: Name the fear
sections.md:
The easiest way to get rid of a fear: ask yourself ==**"What emotions am I feeling right now? Why am I scared?"**==

If I'd asked that when I had to jump into the water from 6 metres:
- I'm really high up, I might hurt myself.
- But the others jumped and didn't get hurt.
- I might jump wrong.
- So might the 13-year-old before me, and he was fine.
- I've run out of reasons not to jump. So let's jump.

That's basically what happened, but it took me about 10 minutes because I didn't ask the questions.

Ali says it's the same with the fear of posting on YouTube. He wanted to post in 2010 and did it in 2017. That's crazy.

sections.title: Nobody is watching you that closely
sections.md:
You live your own life, so you think everybody is looking at you, judging you, caring about you.

At the same time, when I say something to someone I barely think about it, and they might take it deeply.

==I can be whoever I want, because nobody is putting their attention on me. They care about how they look and what they do.==

[[fig:spotlight]]

::: book
Psychologists call it the **spotlight effect** (you called it the "projector" effect). In the classic study, students wore an embarrassing Barry Manilow T-shirt into a room. They guessed about half the room would notice. Only about a quarter did.
:::

sections.title: Alter ego
sections.md:
Develop an alter ego and use it when you need it. I need it most for working hard and not wasting time, and for things like not eating unhealthy stuff. It also works for public speaking.



::: book
This is sometimes called the **Batman effect**: in a 2017 study, kids who pretended to be Batman or another hero kept working on a boring task longer than kids who were just themselves.
:::

When something unpleasant happens (rejected by a girl, by a job), ask:
- Will this matter in **10 minutes**?
- Will this matter in **10 weeks**?
- Will this matter in **10 years**?

So you look at the bigger picture.

ideas: Name the fear and what you're feeling. Most fears run out of reasons once you list them.
Nobody watches you as closely as you think.
Use an alter ego when you need to act differently from your normal self.
Ask whether it will matter in 10 minutes, 10 weeks and 10 years.

chapters.title: Get Started
summary: You don't have to be perfect. Just start: the 5-minute rule and "what's the next step?"
Track your progress, find an accountability buddy, and don't label yourself a procrastinator.
Forgive yourself for past procrastination. People who do procrastinate less next time.

sections.title: You don't have to be perfect
sections.md:
When I don't want to start something because I want to do it well, I think:

==I don't have to do this perfectly. I should just start.==

MrBeast has to make his videos perfect now, but in his first 10 years he didn't. What he had to do was start, and he did. Then he perfected them over time.

I don't have to be perfect yet. Just do it.

sections.title: 4 questions before a task
sections.md:
Get into the habit of asking a few simple questions. Ali asks his team these and encourages them to ask him too:

1. Imagine a week has passed and you still haven't started the task. **What are the three main reasons you haven't?**
2. What can you do to reduce the risk of those three reasons getting in the way?
3. Who can you ask for help to stay on track?
4. ==What one action can you take right now that increases the chance you'll actually finish?==

sections.title: The 5-minute rule
sections.md:
You don't want to do something? Say "I'll do it for 5 minutes."

After 5 minutes you really can stop. Don't force yourself to continue, or you'll learn the rule is a lie. ==Most times, you'll want to keep going.==

sections.title: What's the next step?
sections.md:
One of the world's top experts on procrastination gave Ali the most important advice for doing the thing you want to do: ask yourself ==**"What's the next step?"**==, as in the small step you can take right now.
- Putting off studying for an exam: the next step is opening the page in your textbook.
- Putting off the gym: put your shoes on.
- Putting off writing a script: open Notion.

sections.title: Track your progress
sections.md: Write down your progress and look at it. You see where you're weak and what you are and aren't doing. And you see that you're actually making progress, which is motivating.

sections.title: Accountability buddy
sections.md:
Find a person who holds you accountable for your goals. There's a subreddit, **r/GetMotivatedBuddies**, where you find someone and hold each other accountable. Best if they have the same goal, but it's not required.

For me: I say how often I'm going to upload, and they check that I did.

==Set clear rules at the start==: how often you'll talk, exactly what each of you is supposed to do, how often it's OK to miss, and how strict you'll be with each other.

sections.title: Labels
sections.md:
The way you label yourself is the way you act.

When you're procrastinating, maybe one reason is that you put the wrong label on yourself. Are you a procrastinator? A lazy person? ==No, you aren't.== Remind yourself: I have a goal so clear it's rare for someone my age, and I'm working for it. I went to work to buy a camera, while listening to podcasts about YouTube tactics at work. That's what I'm spending my life on. So yes, I'm a hard-working person. Get to work as always, and don't put a stupid label on yourself.

sections.title: Forgive yourself
sections.md:
"I forgive myself, now I can study" is a study by psychologist Michael Wohl. ==Students who forgave themselves for procrastinating procrastinated less next time.== The ones who stayed angry at themselves procrastinated more: they gave themselves a procrastinator mindset.

If you haven't worked as much as you wanted, forgive yourself, don't dwell on it, work now.

If I feel bad about something I haven't done, I remember something good I have done. Ali does this too: "I didn't do X, but I did do Y."

I'm a harder worker than almost anybody my age. Look at my setup and what I did for it, my YouTube knowledge. Most people my age don't know what their career will be. I decided mine a long time ago and I'm working towards it. ==I 100% forgive myself for every time I've procrastinated. What matters is all the work I've put in.== Now I'll be even better.

You can focus on the small losses, or congratulate yourself on the small wins.

::: check
The study (Wohl, Pychyl and Bennett, 2010) measured procrastination before the next exam, not grades. Self-forgiveness meant less procrastination; it didn't directly show better results.
:::

ideas: You don't need to be perfect. Just start, and improve later.
Before a task, ask what three things would stop you, how to reduce them, who can help, and what one action to take now.
Say "I'll do it for 5 minutes". Then really allow yourself to stop.
Ask "what's the next step?" and make it tiny (open the doc, put on the shoes).
Track your progress and use an accountability buddy with clear rules.
Don't label yourself a procrastinator, and forgive yourself for past delays. That makes you procrastinate less.

chapters.title: Conserve
summary: Burnout comes from doing too much. Say no to anything that doesn't help the channel.
Some distraction is good. Zero breaks leads to burnout; snap back after a short one.
Take breaks when your focus drops, instead of forcing it with "discipline".

sections.title: Say no
sections.md:
One reason for burnout is **hyper-engagement**: saying yes to too much.

Steve Jobs said no to a lot of things Apple could have done. When he came back as CEO, he killed a project the company had worked on for years and cut most of the product line.

> "Saying no is just as important as saying yes."

How to apply it:
- Say "no" more often to anything that doesn't help the channel. Want to get good at chess? No, let me focus on the channel.
-
- If I say yes to everyone and everything, I know what happens: burnout. If I have the channel and not much else to focus on, burnout is harder.

==If you wouldn't do something tomorrow, don't say yes to it for six weeks from now.== You'll probably be busy then too.

sections.title: Controlled distraction and breaks
sections.md:
If you've wasted some time because you were distracted, don't abandon your goals. **Snap back.**

When you focus on something, a little distraction now and then is best:
- Zero distractions = burnout.
- Many or big distractions = no progress.

So control the distraction. Working on the channel and feeling tired? Go outside for 10 minutes, do some push-ups, or listen to one song. Then go back to work.

A study of one workplace found the most productive people worked **52 minutes** and rested **17**. That's resting about a quarter of the time.

[[fig:rest]]

When you lose concentration because you've worked a long time, a break doesn't just make you happier, it makes you work more and better. ==Don't try to "I'm disciplined" your way through a task when you need a break.==

::: check
The 52/17 number comes from DeskTime, a time-tracking app, looking at its own users' data in 2014. It isn't a controlled study, and a later DeskTime update found a different ratio (112 and 26). Take the idea (regular real breaks), not the exact numbers.
:::

sections.title: Doing too many things
sections.md:
One of the main causes of burnout is doing too many things. Like trying to do YouTube while keeping a Duolingo streak, going to a programme every Thursday, juggling a ball 30 minutes a day, learning to cook, and getting good grades, all at once.

If something isn't related to YouTube or the niche, don't force yourself to get good at it (except school grades). You can still have distractions: if something seems interesting, try it. I mean making yourself learn other stuff at the same time and spending discipline on it. That's likely to burn you out.

I already know this, because I don't make myself do other stuff if I don't want to.

ideas: Say no to anything that doesn't help the main goal. If you wouldn't do it tomorrow, don't agree to it for six weeks from now.
Take real breaks when your focus drops, then snap back after distractions instead of giving up.
Doing too many things at once is a main cause of burnout.

chapters.title: Align
summary: Being motivated by the process (intrinsic) beats being motivated by the outcome (extrinsic).
But outcome goals aren't all bad: wanting it for yourself beats doing it so you don't disappoint someone.
Think about the small thing you'll do today, not the big thing it's part of.

sections.title: Intrinsic vs extrinsic motivation
sections.md:
As learned earlier, ==being motivated by liking the process itself (intrinsic) is better than being motivated by the outcome (extrinsic).==

But being motivated by the goal isn't always awful. Compare:
- **Jack** works on his business because he wants to make $1,000,000, so he can be financially free and provide for his family.
- **Mike** works on his business because he wants to make $1,000,000, because otherwise he'd disappoint his dad, who wanted him to become a businessman.

Both focus on the outcome, not the process, but one is still better. Not only is Jack more likely to reach his goal, ==he'll be way happier when he reaches it== than Mike will be.

::: book
Psychologists call Jack's kind *autonomous* motivation (it's his own reason) and Mike's *controlled* (pressure from outside). Research on self-determination theory finds the autonomous kind lasts longer and feels better, even when the goal is the same.
:::

sections.title: Short-term goals
sections.md:
Compare: "I have to make the video and upload it in the next week" vs "I have to edit the intro today" (then something else tomorrow, and in a week it's uploaded).

The second sounds far easier even though it's the same work, and I'm way more likely to start.

==To make yourself work on something, think about the small thing you should do now, not the big thing it's part of.==

ideas: Motivation from the process or your own reasons beats motivation from outside pressure, even when the goal is the same.
Think about the small thing to do today, not the big thing it belongs to.

books.title: Elon Musk
books.author: Walter Isaacson (biography) + videos
books.dek: How he picks missions, builds teams and solves problems. Your notes, grouped by theme.

chapters.title: Mission and mindset
summary: Start with a mission, then find a way to fund it. Pick one that inspires you and is good for the world.
Add to the pie, don't take a piece of it. Do something that wouldn't happen without you.
Find the real limit: how good a video can we make in a week? There's no ceiling on subs.

sections.title: Pick a mission worth fighting for
sections.md:
==We need to do things that inspire us and are good for civilisation, even if the mission seems impossible. Pick a mission worth fighting for.==

He starts with a mission, then finds a way to finance it through a company. His mission was for humans to become a multi-planetary species, so he decided to build rockets.

So for me: I can decide what my mission is, then make a YouTube channel about it.

sections.title: Add to the pie
sections.md:
- Have a mindset of **adding to the pie, not taking a piece of it.** For him the economic pie, for me the YouTube pie.
- Do something that improves the world.
- Read books.
- Find and work with great people.

Having a YouTube channel is like having a child. You don't want your child to starve.

sections.title: Do what wouldn't happen without you
sections.md:
What is the thing you're doing? It's best if it's something that wouldn't happen without you.

If Elon isn't here with the goal of colonising Mars, nobody is. He isn't competing with other people who want to colonise Mars; he's the only one.

==If I can think of a way for the channel to be that nobody else has thought of, and nobody else would think of in the same timeline, that would be great.==

sections.title: Find the limit
sections.md:
- How good a video can we make in 1 week?
- What's the craziest video concept? Where is the limit?

You have no limit. You can grow to a billion subs, so don't put a cap on any of the work. Find the *real* limit: how many people can work on the channel, how long and how well they can work.

sections.title: Read biographies
sections.md:
He reads a lot of biographies. So does MrBeast, and so do a lot of successful people.
