You are the sum of the 5 people you spend the most time with. ==If you read about a successful person, you're spending time with him.==

His only break is intensely playing a strategy video game.

ideas: Start from a mission worth fighting for, then find the way to fund it.
Add to the pie instead of fighting for a piece of it. Do something that wouldn't happen without you.
Look for the real limit instead of an imagined one. Subscriber count has no ceiling, but time and quality do.
Read biographies. Reading about successful people is a way to spend time with them.

chapters.title: Team and leadership
summary: He doesn't befriend his team: friendship makes you soft on bad work. B and C players drag the A players down.
The leader works hardest and stays on the front line. When the troops see the general fighting, they fight.
Write down the channel's values. Hire for attitude: the desire to work maniacally hard.

sections.title: Excellence over friendship
sections.md:
**Extremely important (your words):**

Elon doesn't want to be friends with the people he works with. When you're someone's friend, you don't want to hurt their feelings, so you're less harsh on them. He wants excellence.

How am I going to apply that? I don't know, it's hard. I will be friends with them.

By trying to be nice to people, you're actually not being nice to the other people who do the hard work.

::: key
You don't have to copy him to keep the useful part. Make it a written rule that you judge each other's *work* hard, and the person kindly. Friends who agreed in advance to rip each other's drafts apart get the honesty without losing the friendship. (That's the same as his rule "comradery is dangerous" in chapter 5.)
:::

sections.title: Only A players
sections.md:
**Also very important (your words):**

When one person on the team is a B or C player, he drags the others down. ==Your team needs only A players.== Have an exceptional team.

And an exceptional team needs an even more exceptional leader.

sections.title: The leader works hardest
sections.md:
Musk is the hardest worker, and he's involved in everything.

He slept in the middle of the factory instead of somewhere more private, because in the middle people were more likely to see him. It was less comfortable and gave him zero benefit, but ==it made the team more motivated. When the team sees their leader working hard, they work hard.==

If they see the general out on the battlefield, the troops are motivated. Wherever Napoleon was, that's where his armies did best, Elon said.

One thing he keeps repeating: **be a frontline general.** Stay as close to the work as possible.

sections.title: Stay friends, even after a fight
sections.md:
Elon was pushed out of PayPal, but he kept the relationships. Years later, when SpaceX was about to die, the PayPal founders helped him.

They kicked him out. He could have said "you guys suck", but he didn't. If he had, SpaceX wouldn't exist as a company today, Elon says.

::: book
He was ousted as PayPal's CEO in 2000. In 2008, with SpaceX nearly out of money, Peter Thiel's Founders Fund (PayPal people) invested $20 million.
:::

sections.title: Live with the team
sections.md:
If I want the channel to be highly successful, I need to be with my team. My team can't live in another country.

==If you want a more successful channel, live with the team.==

sections.title: Written values and goals
sections.md:
The channel has to have written values and goals:
- What do we want to achieve?
- How do we achieve it?
- What are our values?

Are we the channel that makes very scientific content? Or the one that makes very high-quality videos but takes a long time? Or something else?

For now, experiment with different ways of making videos. ==At some point, pick exact values, systems, principles, ways of doing things, and goals.==

sections.title: Hire for attitude
sections.md:
The definition of a good attitude is **the desire to work maniacally hard.**

A good attitude is the most important thing when hiring.

sections.title: Give the team a reason
sections.md:
When Elon is building the Tesla robots, he needs the team to work as fast as possible. So he tells them, roughly: our goal is a useful humanoid robot as quickly as possible. That means a future of abundance, a future without poverty. It's a fundamental transformation of civilisation.

Same for robotaxis, roughly: this will be a historically revolutionary product. It will transform everything. People will talk about this moment in a hundred years. It only works if we make tens of millions of them, and I'll work alongside you to make it possible.

==That's how he drives the team to go as fast as possible: a huge reason, plus "I'll be right there with you".==

ideas: Judge the work hard and the person kindly. Agree on that rule in advance.
One weak teammate drags the whole team down, so aim for only strong people.
The leader works hardest and stays close to the work, because the team copies what it sees.
Stay on good terms with people even after a fight. You may need them later.
Write down your channel's values and goals once your experiments show what works.
Hire for attitude (willing to work hard). Skills can be taught.
Give the team a big reason, and work next to them.

chapters.title: How he thinks
summary: To solve a hard problem: dark, silent, alone. Let your mind wander for 20 minutes or a whole night.
Find bottlenecks, keep asking why until you hit the root cause, then delete and simplify.
He takes lessons from everything: sci-fi, games, toys, military history.

sections.title: Think in silence and darkness
sections.md:
How Elon and other successful people solve complex problems:

**Isolate yourself. Make it dark** (so you don't see anything) **and silent** (go somewhere quiet, or use earplugs or white noise).

- Do it for 20 minutes, 30 minutes, an hour, even 5 hours.
- Or stare at an empty wall in silence.

Then you can actually think. You don't have to force yourself to solve it. Just see where your mind goes, and wonder about the thing. ==You're far more likely to reach an answer than in a fast-paced, high-dopamine environment.==

Elon sometimes sits and stares at the wall the entire night. Other times he says "I need to sit alone in silence with no light", goes off to think, and that's where some of his best decisions were made.

sections.title: Bottlenecks and root causes
sections.md:
A lot of the value from the book:
1. **Find bottlenecks.**
2. **Keep asking why** until you get to the root cause.
3. Then **delete and simplify.**

sections.title: Learn from everything
sections.md: Elon takes lessons from everything around him: how humans use their eyes to drive, how toys are manufactured. He gets countless ideas from science-fiction books, games and movies. He takes examples from history, and he's applied military history to car production.

ideas: To solve hard problems, sit alone in silence and darkness and let your mind wander.
Find the bottleneck, keep asking why until you reach the root cause, then delete and simplify.
Take lessons from everything: games, toys, history, sci-fi.

chapters.title: Principles
summary: Extreme urgency: "If we are slow, we are dead."
Simplify everything, which also makes it faster.
Be hardcore: big goals, tight deadlines, and principles simple enough for everyone to apply.

sections.title: Extreme urgency
sections.md:
**1. Extreme urgency** (like MrBeast).
- How can we move faster? Do it faster. Move fast.
- ==A repeated idea, over and over: if we are slow, we are dead.==

**2. Simplify.**
- Make this simpler (which also makes it faster). How can we do it more easily and faster?

sections.title: Hardcore
sections.md:
Elon is very hardcore. One of his favourite words is *hardcore*.
- Big goals, tight deadlines.
- Move fast, work hard, be hardcore.

He makes it really easy for employees to understand the company's principles and apply them.

ideas: Work with urgency. Ask how to move faster, and simplify, which also speeds things up.
Set big goals with tight deadlines, and keep principles simple enough that everyone can apply them.

chapters.title: The algorithm
summary: His 5 steps, in this exact order: question, delete, simplify, speed up, automate.
If you don't add back at least 10% of what you deleted, you didn't delete enough.
Plus his company rules: hands-on leaders, no comfortable comradery, attitude over skills, laws of physics only.

sections.title: The 5-step algorithm
sections.md:
Elon has what he calls **the algorithm**. He repeats it over and over, to the point where it gets annoying.

[[fig:algorithm]]

1. **Question every requirement.** Why does this have to be done like this?
2. **Delete any part of the process you can.** You might have to add some back later. ==If you didn't add back at least 10%, you didn't delete enough.==
3. **Simplify and optimise.** Only after step 2: you don't want to optimise a process that shouldn't exist.
4. **Accelerate cycle time.** Any process can be sped up, but only *after* the first three steps.
5. **Automate.** That comes last.

::: check
Your notes had steps 4 and 5 the wrong way round ("before"). In Isaacson's book they come *after*: speed up only once you've questioned, deleted and simplified, and automate last. His big lesson from Tesla was that he'd automated things that should have been deleted.
:::

::: key
For your videos: before you speed up editing or automate anything, ask which steps of your workflow (shots, B-roll, graphics) could be deleted entirely.
:::

sections.title: The company rules
sections.md:
And a sub-algorithm for how the company should be:

1. **All technical leaders must have hands-on experience.** If I'm your boss, I need to have done your job and understand it deeply. Otherwise you're like a Roman general who can't use a sword.
2. **Comradery is dangerous.** It makes it hard for people to challenge each other's work. We're only around 5 people, so we'll be friends, but make it a core value to judge each other's work.
3. **It's OK to be wrong. Just don't be confident and wrong.**
4. **Never ask your troops to do something you're not willing to do.**
5. **When hiring, look for the right attitude.** Skills can be taught. Changing an attitude requires a brain transplant.
6. **A maniacal sense of urgency is our operating principle.**
7. **The only rules are the ones dictated by the laws of physics** (and the local law). Everything else is a recommendation.

ideas: The algorithm, in this order: question every requirement, delete, simplify, speed up, automate.
If you don't have to add back at least 10% of what you deleted, you didn't delete enough.
Don't speed up or automate a step that shouldn't exist. Apply this to your editing workflow.
Company rules: leaders must have done the work, challenge each other's work, be wrong but never confident and wrong, and never ask others to do what you wouldn't.

chapters.title: Polytopia life lessons
summary: Play life like a game, and don't fear losing. After 50 losses you play with less emotion and more risk.
Be proactive: you never win unless you set the strategy.
You only get so many turns. Optimise every one.

sections.title: Polytopia life lessons
sections.md:
Elon plays the strategy game Polytopia. Lessons drawn from it:

1. **Empathy is not an asset.**
2. **Play life like a game.**
3. **Don't fear losing.** You will lose. It hurts the first 50 times. When you get used to losing, you play each game with less emotion, you're more fearless, and you take more risks.
4. **Be proactive.** You'll never win unless you take charge of setting the strategy.
5. **Optimise every turn.** In the game you only get about 30 turns, so you optimise each one. In life you also get a set number of turns. ==If you let a few slide, we'll never get to Mars.== (For me: we'll never get to helping a million people improve themselves.)

::: key
Lesson 1 doesn't fit your channel: empathy is literally your product. The viewer has to feel you get him. Read it as "don't let feelings stop a hard decision", and keep the empathy for the viewer.
:::

ideas: Treat life like a game and don't fear losing. Losing gets easier and you take more risks.
Be proactive. You only win if you set the strategy.
You get a limited number of turns, so make each one count.

books.title: Huberman Lab
books.author: Andrew Huberman (podcast)
books.dek: What you should actually start doing, and the rest. Your notes, with fact checks.

chapters.title: What I should actually start doing
summary: Resist urges. Learn to love the hard work itself; don't do it for a reward.
Focus practice: eyes closed, attention on your breath and body.
Morning light in the first hour, water when you wake up, fewer screens before bed.

sections.title: Resisting urges
sections.md:
When you look at the tasty unhealthy food and don't buy it, that also trains you not to argue with people and not to open Instagram. ==In life, the more you resist urges, the better you get at it.== It's so important.

If you only get one thing from the Huberman podcast, make it this.

::: check
The idea that resisting one urge trains self-control everywhere is shakier than it sounds. Big reviews of "self-control training" studies find small effects that shrink further once weak studies are removed. What's better supported: changing your environment (don't keep the junk food around, log out of Instagram) and building habits so you need less willpower in the first place.
:::

sections.title: How to do hard work
sections.md:
When you're doing the hard work, don't think about the reward. ==The hard work is the reward. Learn to love it.==

Have a growth mindset: you do hard work, you love hard work, and hard work makes you grow. It's THE thing that makes you grow.

Don't spike dopamine right before or after effort (no "I'll scroll after this"). Learn to get the good feeling from the effort itself.

Remember Ali Abdaal's reward study. Huberman talks about a different one: kids who liked drawing and did it often. Teachers started giving them awards for drawing (a gold star, a certificate), then stopped. ==Afterwards the kids drew way less than before the rewards.== They'd learned it was something you do for the reward.

[[fig:rewards]]

That's why I shouldn't "run 5 km for the reward of a cake". I'll quit.

::: check
The drawing study is real (Lepper, Greene and Nisbett, 1973) and the numbers above are from it. The part about effort "raising your baseline dopamine" is Huberman's explanation, not something measured in people. The behaviour advice still stands.
:::

sections.title: How to focus
sections.md:
Do this sometimes: close your eyes and focus on your breathing and on where your skin touches things. Just internal focus on your body.

It actually really helps. Even if you do it once, it still helps long-term.

::: check
The study Huberman cites (Basso and others, 2019) used **13 minutes a day for 8 weeks**; you wrote 17. Attention, memory and mood improved at 8 weeks but not at 4. So it's a daily habit, not something that works long-term after one session.
:::

sections.title: Morning sunlight
sections.md:
Whenever you read this, actually try it: ==go outside in the first hour after waking==, or at least open the window and stick your head out. 5 to 20 minutes is good.

It helps with several things, including testosterone, being more productive during the day, and being happier.

::: check
The strongest evidence is for your body clock: morning light helps you get sleepy at the right time at night and feel awake in the day. Outside light is far brighter than indoor light, even when it's cloudy. The testosterone claim is weak, so leave that one out of a video.
:::

sections.title: Water when you wake up
sections.md:
Drink **500 ml to 1 L of water** when you wake up.

It's not just for debloating. It tells your body it's awake, and it helps with a lot of things.

::: check
The simple, solid reason: you've gone all night without drinking, so it rehydrates you. "Tells your body it's awake" is more of a figure of speech; light is the main thing that sets your body clock.
:::

sections.title: Screens at night
sections.md:
Limit late-night screens. At least limit screens without blue-light glasses in the hour before bed. Limiting screens in general is even better, but my work matters more than this, so lower the brightness and blue light when possible.

::: check
Blue-light glasses haven't been shown to improve sleep in good reviews. What helps more: dim the screen and the room, and avoid stuff that gets you wound up right before bed.
:::

ideas: Do hard things without a reward. The effort is the point, and rewards can make you quit when they stop.
Change your environment (don't keep junk food around, log out) instead of relying on willpower.
Train focus daily with a few minutes of eyes-closed attention on your breath and body.
Get outside light in the first hour after waking.
Drink water when you wake up.
Dim screens and the room before bed.

chapters.title: Other stuff (just info)
summary: Cold exposure, and any hard thing you don't quit, teaches your brain to do hard things.
The eye-movement trick for falling asleep fast.

sections.title: Doing hard things
sections.md:
Cold exposure is good because it teaches you to do hard things.

==Anything hard I do without quitting teaches my brain to do hard things without quitting.== The opposite is also true.

sections.title: How to fall asleep fast
sections.md:
For some reason, you need to forget your body's physical position.

Close your eyes. With your eyes closed, move them (not your head): left, right, up, down, spin counter-clockwise, spin clockwise. Then do a long exhale. Repeat 3 times.

::: check
I couldn't find a study behind this one. It's harmless to try, but don't teach it as science.
:::

ideas: Anything hard that you don't quit teaches you to do hard things.
Eye movements and a long exhale to fall asleep: harmless to try, but there's no study behind it.

books.title: How to Sell on YouTube
books.author: Ali Abdaal (podcast) + your own thinking
books.dek: Niche, offer, promise, and why trust comes before any sale.

chapters.title: The offer
summary: Don't sell a $10 thing to 1,000 people. Sell a $1,000 thing to 10 people who have money.
Niche + offer + promise. Expensive buyers want results with the least effort, not more information.
Video courses are dead: YouTube videos are free courses.

sections.title: Sell high-ticket
sections.md:
==Don't sell a $10 thing to 1,000 people. Sell a $1,000 thing to 10 people.==

People don't care about video courses anymore. YouTube videos are free courses.

Sell something people would pay a lot of money for. Becoming more attractive is something people actually pay for.

sections.title: Sell to people who have money
sections.md:
If I sell attractiveness coaching to a guy making $1,500 a month, he won't pay $1,000 a month for it. A guy making $80,000 a month will.

So maybe my niche should be for people a bit older, like 20, or I'll just gradually raise the age as I get older.

And make videos for people with money. Nothing weird, just not "skincare routine under $20" or "the cheapest X". Not the cheapest food, the healthiest, easiest food to cook.

::: key
You don't need to decide the age now. Your own notes say sell only once you have views and trust, and ask the audience what they want first. Their answers will tell you the age and the price.
:::

sections.title: Niche, offer, promise
sections.md:
Step 1: figure out the niche and the offer.
- **Niche:** attractiveness for young guys.
- **Offer:** I'll help you become more attractive.

You also need a **promise**, for example "I'll help you become an 8/10 by month 3".

In high-ticket sales, people don't want more, they want less: ==more value with less information, and faster results.== If you can make them an 8/10 in 1 month instead of 3, they prefer that.
- Cheap product: they want as many things as possible.
- Expensive product: they want as much value as possible with the least effort.

So results are what matter. If they can get the results more easily, better. Having to watch 150 hours of courses to get them is worse.

::: check
Careful with a promise like "8/10 by month 3". You can't control genetics, and a promise you can't keep destroys the trust your notes say matters most. Promise what you control: the routine, the inputs, the support ("a 90-day plan for skin, hair and body, with weekly check-ins").
:::

ideas: Sell a high-priced thing to a few people instead of a cheap thing to many.
Sell to people who have the money, and make videos for them.
You need a niche, an offer and a promise. Promise what you control (the plan and support), not outcomes like genetics.
Expensive buyers want results with the least effort, not more information.

chapters.title: Videos and trust
summary: Every video should bring the viewer one step closer to his goal, and make him trust you more.
The audience must have money, a reason to buy, and exist in big numbers.
Like a story: they need to know the character before they care. Video → longer video → Discord → cheap product → coaching.

sections.title: Videos aligned with what you sell
sections.md:
The videos should be aligned with what you're selling. The target audience should:
1. Have enough money.
2. Have enough reason to buy your thing.
3. Exist (a big TAM: total addressable market).

sections.title: Trust and authenticity
sections.md:
Every video should bring them ==one step closer to their desired outcome== (becoming more attractive).

And they need to trust you as much as possible. Ask yourself: **"Does this make them trust me more or less?"** Trust and authenticity are really important. They need to see my personality and trust me so I can bring them closer.

As soon as I get views, I should sell something (if I want money). If I'm not ready to have a product, sell 1 hour of my time on a call. If I have a product, price it high.

You can sell a cheap or free product, like my Discord, that then leads to the expensive product.

sections.title: Selling is like a video story
sections.md:
(From my own knowledge.)

Selling an expensive product is like a YouTube video story. If the character has a big problem at minute 1 and overcomes it at minute 2, you're way less invested than if he has the problem at minute 17 and overcomes it with hard work at minute 34.

==People won't care about my coaching if they don't know me.== You need to know the character before you cheer for him.

[[fig:funnel]]

So they watch a video, then a longer video, then join the Discord, engage, get a cheap product, and then my expensive coaching. If I make one short video and push expensive coaching, nobody buys unless they already know me.

ideas: Every video should move the viewer one step closer to his goal and make him trust you more.
The audience needs money, a reason to buy and to exist in large numbers.
People need to know you before they care. Build the path: video, longer video, Discord, cheap product, then coaching.

chapters.title: Starting out
summary: At first, do things that don't scale: talk to potential customers, get on calls.
You DON'T know what the customer wants. Ask them before you build anything.

sections.title: Do things that don't scale
sections.md:
At first, do things that aren't scalable. Chat with potential customers, have calls with them, put time into non-scalable things at the start. Then you get a few customers and scale from there.

At the start, the Airbnb founders went around taking photos of the apartments themselves, because regular people took bad photos. Not scalable, but it gave them the first push.

sections.title: You don't know what the customer wants
sections.md:
==You DON'T know what the customer wants.== Before you build a big product and start selling it, learn what the customer wants, because it is NOT what you think.

So ask them. Ask your audience in different ways before creating the product.

ideas: At the start, do things that don't scale: talk to people and get on calls.
You don't know what customers want. Ask them before you build anything.

books.title: Thumbnail Tutorial
books.author: Video notes
books.dek: What the viewer should feel, where to find 10+ references, and how to study them.

chapters.title: Thumbnails
summary: Start from what the viewer should feel. The thumbnail must spark curiosity on its own, then work with the title.
Collect 10+ references from 5 places, and ask 3 questions about each one.
Novelty, strong contrast, light edges for dark mode, and zero clutter.

sections.title: What should the viewer feel?
sections.md:
For thumbnails, think about ==what the viewer wants to feel.==

Think about it on its own, then as a combo with the title. It needs to spark enough instant curiosity on its own that the person looks at it and then reads the title.

sections.title: 10+ references from 5 places
sections.md:
You need around **10+ inspirations** for your thumbnail:
1. Your own outlier videos
2. Random channels' outlier videos
3. Outlier videos from people in your niche who cover a **different** topic
4. Thumbnails that caught your eye
5. Off-platform: posters, billboards

sections.title: The 3 questions
sections.md:
Put your reference thumbnails in a playlist or somewhere you can view them together. Then ask these 3 questions to understand how they work underneath:

1. ==What questions, if any, does this make me ask?==
2. ==What emotions, if any, does this make me feel?==
3. **How** does this reference make me ask those questions or feel those emotions?

::: key
Question 3 is the one that turns copying into learning. "Big shocked face" is what it does; "the face reacts to something I can't see yet" is how it works, and that you can reuse with your own topic.
:::

sections.title: Random tips
sections.md:
- **Novelty.** Think about what's new when making a thumbnail.
- **Dark mode.** Most people have YouTube in dark mode, so a white background, or at least light colour around the edges, is good.
- **Contrast and colour.** Strong contrast and colours. They're usually exaggerated in thumbnails, and they should be.
- ==**Remove ALL clutter.**== Even if your room naturally has a lot of stuff in the background, the viewer's eyes need to land easily on what matters.

::: check
I don't know of a public number for how many viewers use dark mode, so don't rely on "most". Your Thumb Lab showed light backgrounds are rare in your niche (most thumbnails are dark or mid-tone), so a light one stands out either way. It also recommended a deeper cream rather than pure white, so it still holds up for light-mode viewers.
:::

ideas: Start from what the viewer should feel, and make the thumbnail spark curiosity on its own before the title does.
Collect 10 or more references from five places, including your own outliers and off-platform posters.
For each reference ask what question it raises, what emotion it creates, and how it does that.
Use novelty, strong contrast, light edges for dark mode, and no clutter.
